topics.title: Arithmetic, Assignment and Unary Operators
topics.summary: Operators combine values into expressions: math, assignment, increment/decrement and type conversion.
topics.description:
An **expression** is any piece of code that produces a value. It is built from **operands** (the values) and **operators** (the symbols). For `5 + 3`, the operands are `5` and `3` and the operator is `+`.

### Arithmetic
`+ - * / % **` (add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, exponent). `%` gives the remainder (`17 % 5` is `2`) and is perfect for even/odd checks and wrapping around. `**` was added in ES2016 (`2 ** 5` is `32`).

### Assignment
`=` assigns. Compound forms update in place: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`. Modern versions add logical assignment `||=`, `&&=` and `??=`.

### Unary operators (one operand)
- `+x` converts to number, `-x` negates.
- `typeof x`, `!x`, `delete obj.key`, `void 0`.
- `++x` / `--x` (**prefix**): change first, then return the new value.
- `x++` / `x--` (**postfix**): return the old value, then change.

```js
let x = 5;
let y = x++; // y = 5, x = 6
let z = ++x; // x = 7, z = 7
```

### Operator precedence
`**` binds tighter than `* /`, which bind tighter than `+ -`. Use parentheses to make intent obvious: `(a + b) * c`.

### Floating point precision
Numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. For money, work in the smallest unit (paise/cents) or use `toFixed()` only for display.
keyPoints: % returns remainder, ** is exponent
Prefix ++x returns the new value, postfix x++ returns the old one
Unary + converts to number: +"5" is 5
0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 because of floating point
Use parentheses instead of memorising precedence
pitfalls: Dividing by 0 gives Infinity, not an exception
toFixed returns a string, not a number

examples.title: Prefix vs postfix

interview.q: What is the difference between x++ and ++x?
interview.a: Both add 1. x++ returns the value before the increment, ++x returns the value after the increment.
Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance (Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON) or use integers.
It converts its operand to a number, so +"5" is 5, +true is 1 and +"abc" is NaN.

topics.title: Comparison and Equality (== vs ===)
topics.summary: Prefer === (strict equality); know exactly what == coerces and when Object.is differs.
topics.description:
Comparison operators return a **boolean**: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`.

### Loose equality `==`
Converts types before comparing, using a complicated set of rules. `5 == "5"` is `true`, `0 == false` is `true`, `null == undefined` is `true`.

### Strict equality `===`
Compares **type and value** with no conversion. `5 === "5"` is `false`. This is what you want almost always.

### Special cases
- `NaN === NaN` is `false`.
- `+0 === -0` is `true`.
- `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true` and `Object.is(+0, -0)` is `false` - it is the "same value" check.
- Objects, arrays and functions are compared by **reference**: `{} === {}` is `false`.
- `null == 0` is `false` but `null >= 0` is `true` (relational operators convert null to 0, equality does not).

### Relational comparisons
- Strings compare **alphabetically** by UTF-16 code: `"apple" < "banana"` and `"10" < "9"` (string compare!).
- Mixed string and number: the string is converted to a number.
- Chained comparisons do not work like maths: `1 < 5 < 3` is `true` because `(1 < 5)` becomes `true`, then `true < 3` is `1 < 3`.

### Rule of thumb
Use `===` and `!==`. The only common use of `==` is `value == null`, which checks `null` or `undefined` together.
keyPoints: === checks type and value, == coerces first
Objects/arrays compare by reference
NaN is not equal to itself, use Number.isNaN or Object.is
value == null is true for both null and undefined
Strings compare alphabetically, not numerically
pitfalls: 2 < 12 < 5 is true because of left-to-right evaluation
"10" > "9" is false (string comparison) but 10 > "9" is true
[] == false is true and [] is truthy at the same time

examples.title: Equality gallery

interview.a: == converts operands to a common type before comparing; === compares both type and value and never converts.

interview.q: What is the output of console.log(2 < 12 < 5)?
interview.a: true. 2 < 12 is true, then true is coerced to 1 and 1 < 5 is true.

interview.q: How are two objects compared in JavaScript?
interview.a: By reference. Two separate objects with the same content are not equal; only two variables pointing to the same object are equal.

topics.title: Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting
topics.summary: &&, || and ! return one of their operands, which enables default values and guard patterns.
topics.description:
The logical operators are `&&` (AND), `||` (OR) and `!` (NOT). With booleans they behave as in school logic, but with other types they have an important twist: **`&&` and `||` return one of the operands, not necessarily a boolean.**

### Rules
- `a || b` returns `a` if `a` is truthy, otherwise `b`.
- `a && b` returns `a` if `a` is falsy, otherwise `b`.
- `!a` always returns a boolean.

### Short-circuit evaluation
The right side runs only when needed. That makes these patterns common:

```js
const name = userInput || "Guest";        // default value
user && user.login();                     // run only if user exists
const isAdult = age >= 18 && hasId;       // combine conditions
```

### Nullish coalescing `??`
`||` treats `0`, `""` and `false` as "missing". `??` only treats `null` and `undefined` as missing, so it is safer for defaults:

```js
const count = 0;
count || 10;   // 10 (wrong if 0 is valid)
count ?? 10;   // 0
```

### Logical assignment (ES2021)
`a ||= b`, `a &&= b`, `a ??= b` assign only when the short-circuit rule says so.

### Mixing
You cannot mix `??` with `||` or `&&` without parentheses. `&&` has higher precedence than `||`.
keyPoints: && and || return an operand, not always a boolean
|| gives the first truthy value, && gives the first falsy value
Use ?? when 0, "" or false are valid values
||=, &&= and ??= are logical assignment shortcuts
Short-circuit stops evaluation early
pitfalls: Using || for defaults breaks when 0 or "" is legitimate input
a ?? b || c is a syntax error without parentheses

examples.title: Defaults and guards

interview.a: 0. && runs first: "hi" && 0 is 0. Then null || 0 returns the last operand, 0.
|| falls back for any falsy value (0, "", false...). ?? falls back only for null and undefined.
The second operand of && or || is evaluated only if the first operand does not already decide the result.

topics.summary: Choose which code runs using if/else chains, switch statements and the ternary operator.
keyPoints: if/else chains run the first truthy branch only
switch uses === and needs break to avoid fall-through
Ternary is an expression, if is a statement
default handles the no-match case
An object lookup can replace a big switch
pitfalls: Forgetting break causes fall-through to following cases
switch(true) tricks and deep nested ternaries hurt readability
Declaring let/const directly inside a case without braces shares one scope

examples.title: Switch and ternary
Voting eligibility with early returns

interview.q: Why do we write break in switch?
interview.a: Without break, execution continues into the next case (fall-through). break exits the switch after the matching case runs.
Strict equality (===), so switch("5") will not match case 5.

interview.q: When should you use the ternary operator?
interview.a: For short two-way choices that produce a value, such as assigning or returning. Use if/else when you need multiple statements or complex logic.

topics.title: Loops: for, while, do-while, break and continue
topics.summary: Repeat work with for, while and do...while and control the flow with break and continue.
topics.description:
Loops execute a block of code repeatedly while a condition is true.

### for
```js
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { console.log(i); }
```
Three parts: **initialisation**, **condition** (checked before every run), **update** (after every run). Any part can be left empty; `for (;;) {}` is an infinite loop.

### while
Use when you do not know the number of iterations upfront:
```js
let n = 1;
while (n <= 10) { n++; }
```

### do...while
Runs the body **at least once**, then checks the condition. Good for "ask, then validate" flows.

### break, continue and labels
- `break` leaves the loop completely.
- `continue` skips to the next iteration.
- A **label** lets you break out of nested loops: `outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }`.

### Common practice problems
Times tables, sum 1 to N, prime check, leap year, star patterns. Use `let` in loops: each iteration gets its own binding, which matters for closures and callbacks.

### Choosing a loop
- Known count: `for`.
- Unknown count / waiting for a condition: `while`.
- Run once first: `do...while`.
- Iterating arrays: `for...of`, `forEach` or `map` (see arrays).
keyPoints: for = init; condition; update
do...while always runs at least once
break exits the loop, continue skips one iteration
Labels allow breaking out of nested loops
Always make sure the condition eventually becomes false
pitfalls: Infinite loops from forgetting to update the counter
Using var in a loop with async callbacks shares one variable

examples.title: Table, sum and prime
Star pattern, break/continue and label

interview.a: while checks the condition before each iteration and may never run. do...while runs the body once first and checks the condition afterwards.

interview.q: What is the difference between break and continue?
interview.a: break terminates the whole loop; continue stops only the current iteration and moves to the next one.

interview.q: How do you exit from nested loops at once?
interview.a: Use a labelled break (break outer;), or put the loops in a function and return.

topics.title: for...in vs for...of vs forEach
topics.summary: for...of iterates values of iterables, for...in iterates enumerable keys of objects.
topics.description:
Three similar-looking ways to loop over collections often confuse beginners.

### for...of
Iterates over the **values** of any **iterable**: arrays, strings, Map, Set, NodeList, generators. You can use `break`, `continue` and `await` inside.

```js
for (const fruit of ["apple", "mango"]) console.log(fruit);
for (const ch of "JS") console.log(ch);
```

### for...in
Iterates over the **enumerable property keys** (as strings) of an object, **including inherited ones**. Use it for plain objects, and prefer `Object.keys/entries` for arrays.

```js
for (const key in { a: 1, b: 2 }) console.log(key);
```

### Array.prototype.forEach
Calls a function for each element. It returns `undefined`, cannot be stopped with `break`, and does not wait for `async` callbacks.

### Which one to use
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| values of an array/string/Map/Set | `for...of` |
| keys of a plain object | `Object.keys` / `Object.entries` + `for...of` |
| side effects for every item, no early exit | `forEach` |
| early exit | `for...of` / `some` / `every` / classic `for` |
| `await` inside | `for...of` |

### Remember
Plain objects are **not iterable**: `for (const x of {a:1})` throws a TypeError. Use `Object.entries(obj)` first.
keyPoints: for...of gives values, for...in gives keys (strings)
for...in also walks the prototype chain
Plain objects are not iterable - use Object.entries
forEach cannot break or await properly
Use for...of when you need break or await
pitfalls: Using for...in on arrays gives string indexes and may include extra properties
forEach(async ...) does not wait for the promises
Adding to an array while iterating with for...of can cause endless loops

examples.title: Compare the three loops

interview.a: for...in loops over enumerable keys (including inherited ones) as strings. for...of loops over values of an iterable object.

interview.q: Can you use break inside forEach?
interview.a: No. forEach cannot be stopped except by throwing. Use a for...of loop, or some()/every() for early exit.

interview.q: Why does for...of fail on a plain object?
interview.a: Plain objects do not implement Symbol.iterator. Convert with Object.keys, Object.values or Object.entries.
